steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Zero-shot coordination (ZSC) is a major challenge of cooperative AI: training agents that are able to coordinate with a wide range of unseen partners. The traditional method is self-play (SP), which involves iteratively improving strategies by playing against oneself. SP can converge to an equilibrium of the game, but the strategies often form specific behaviours and conventions to get higher payoffs. So a fully converged SP strategy may not be able to adapt to coordinating with unseen strategies.

To overcome these limitations of SP, most ZSC methods focus on promoting strategic or behavioural diversity, by introducing population-based training (PBT) to improve the adaptive ability of the strategies. PBT aims to improve the cooperative outcomes with the other strategies in the population, in order to promote zero-shot coordination with unseen strategies. It does this by maintaining a set of strategies to break the conventions of SP and by optimizing the rewards for each pair in the population. Most state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods try to pre-train a diverse population or introduce hand-crafted methods, and these are used to master cooperative games by optimizing fixed objectives within the population. These methods have been shown to be effective for intricate cooperative tasks like Overcooked and Hanabi.

However, when a fixed population-level objective is optimized, for example the expected rewards within the population, the coordination ability of the strategies within the population may not be improved. That is, the overall performance may improve, but the coordination ability within the population may not be promoted at the same time. We call this phenomenon “cooperative incompatibility”, and it shows that it is important to consider the trade-offs between overall performance and coordination ability when trying to optimize a fixed population-level objective.

  - proof: converges to optimal strategy, Q-sublinear rate with in-degree centrality as preference metric

  - solver: Shapley value -> adaptive ability of strategies, cooperative incompatibility distribution

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Zero-shot coordination (ZSC) is a major challenge of cooperative AI: training agents that are able to coordinate with a wide range of unseen partners. The traditional method is self-play (SP), which involves iteratively improving strategies by playing against oneself. SP can converge to an equilibrium of the game, but the strategies often form specific behaviours and conventions to get higher payoffs. So a fully converged SP strategy may not be able to adapt to coordinating with unseen strategies.

To overcome these limitations of SP, most ZSC methods focus on promoting strategic or behavioural diversity, by introducing population-based training (PBT) to improve the adaptive ability of the strategies. PBT aims to improve the cooperative outcomes with the other strategies in the population, in order to promote zero-shot coordination with unseen strategies. It does this by maintaining a set of strategies to break the conventions of SP and by optimizing the rewards for each pair in the population. Most state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods try to pre-train a diverse population or introduce hand-crafted methods, and these are used to master cooperative games by optimizing fixed objectives within the population. These methods have been shown to be effective for intricate cooperative tasks like Overcooked and Hanabi.

However, when a fixed population-level objective is optimized, for example the expected rewards within the population, the coordination ability of the strategies within the population may not be improved. That is, the overall performance may improve, but the coordination ability within the population may not be promoted at the same time. We call this phenomenon “cooperative incompatibility”, and it shows that it is important to consider the trade-offs between overall performance and coordination ability when trying to optimize a fixed population-level objective.

To address the problem of cooperative incompatibility we reformulate cooperative tasks as Graphic-Form Games (GFGs). In GFGs the strategies are nodes, and the weight of the edge between two nodes is the mean cooperative payoff of the two strategies. We also use sub-graphs of GFGs, which we call preference Graphic-Form Games (P-GFGs), to further profile the maximum cooperative payoff of each node within the graph, and this lets us evaluate cooperative incompatibility and identify the strategies that fail to collaborate. We then propose the Cooperative Open-ended LEarning (COLE) framework, which iteratively generates a new strategy that approximates the best response to the empirical gamescapes of P-GFGs. We have proved that the COLE framework can converge to the optimal strategy with a Q-sublinear rate when in-degree centrality is used as the preference evaluation metric.

To put the COLE framework into practice against cooperative incompatibility, we implement a practical algorithm \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}}, which combines the Shapley Value solution with our GFG. \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} consists of a simulator, a solver, and a trainer, and it is designed specifically to master cooperative tasks with two players. The solver uses the intuitive solution concept of the Shapley value to evaluate the adaptive ability of the strategies and to calculate the cooperative incompatibility distribution. The trainer tries to approximate the best responses to the cooperative incompatibility distribution mixture in the most recent population. To evaluate the performance of \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} we ran experiments in Overcooked, which is a two-player cooperative task environment. We evaluated the adaptive ability of \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} by testing it against partners of different levels, middle-level and expert unseen partners. The middle-level partner is a commonly used behavior cloning model, and the expert partners are the strategies of current methods, i.e., SP, PBT, FCP, and MEP, and our proposed \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}}. The experiments showed that \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} outperforms the recent SOTA methods in both evaluation protocols. Also, the analysis of GFGs and P-GFGs over the learning process of \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} showed that the framework overcomes cooperative incompatibility efficiently. Our contributions can be summarized as follows.

- We introduce Graphic-Form Games (GFGs) and Preference Graphic-Form Games (P-GFGs) to reformulate cooperative tasks in an intuitive way, which lets us evaluate and identify cooperative incompatibility during learning more efficiently.

- We develop graphic-form gamescapes to help understand the objective, and we present the COLE framework, which iteratively approximates the best responses preferred by most others.

- We prove that the algorithm converges to the optimal strategy, with a Q-sublinear convergence rate when in-degree preference centrality is used. Empirical experiments in the game Overcooked verify that the proposed algorithm is effective compared to SOTA methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Zero-shot coordination (ZSC) is a major challenge of cooperative AI to train agents that have the ability to coordinate with a wide range of unseen partners [1,2]. The traditional method of self-play (SP) [3] involves improving strategies iteratively by playing against oneself. While SP can converge to an equilibrium of the game [4], the strategies often form specific behaviours and conventions to achieve higher payoffs [2]. As a result, a fully converged SP strategy may not be adaptable to coordinating with unseen strategies [5,2].

To overcome the limitations of SP, most ZSC methods focus on promoting strategic or behavioural diversity by introducing population-based training (PBT) to improve strategies’ adaptive ability [6,7,8,9]. PBT aims to improve cooperative outcomes with other strategies in the population to promote zero-shot coordination with unseen strategies. This is achieved by maintaining a set of strategies to break the conventions of SP [3] and optimizing the rewards for each pair in the population. Most state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods attempt to pre-train a diverse population [10,9] or introduce hand-crafted methods [7,8], which are used to master cooperative games by optimizing fixed objectives within the population. These methods have been shown to be effective in addressing intricate cooperative tasks such as Overcooked [6] and Hanabi [11].

However, when optimizing a fixed population-level objective, such as expected rewards within population [10,9,8], the coordination ability of strategies within the population may not be improved. Specifically, while overall performance may improve, the coordination ability within the population may not be promoted in a simultaneous manner. This phenomenon, which we term “cooperative incompatibility”, highlights the importance of considering the trade-offs between overall performance and coordination ability when attempting to optimize a fixed population-level objective.

In addressing the problem of cooperative incompatibility, we reformulate cooperative tasks as Graphic-Form Games (GFGs). In GFGs, strategies are characterized as nodes, with the weight of the edges between nodes representing the mean cooperative payoffs of the two associated strategies. Additionally, by utilizing sub-graphs of GFGs referred to as preference Graphic-Form Games (P-GFGs), we are able to further profile each node’s maximum cooperative payoff within the graph, enabling us to evaluate cooperative incompatibility and identify strategies that fail to collaborate. We then propose the Cooperative Open-ended LEarning (COLE) framework, which iteratively generates a new strategy that approximates the best response to the empirical gamescapes of P-GFGs. We have proved that the COLE framework can converge to the optimal strategy with a Q-sublinear rate when using in-degree centrality as the preference evaluation metric.

To put the COLE framework into practice against cooperative incompatibility, we implement a practical algorithm \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} by combining the Shapley Value solution [12] with our GFG. \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} comprises a simulator, a solver, and a trainer, designed to master cooperative tasks with two players specifically. The solver, utilizing the development of the intuitive solution concept Shapley value, evaluates the adaptive ability of strategies and calculates the cooperative incompatibility distribution. The trainer aims to approximate the best responses to the cooperative incompatibility distribution mixture in the most recent population. To evaluate the performance of the \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}}, we conducted experiments in Overcooked, a two-player cooperative task environment [6]. We evaluated the adaptive ability of \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} by testing its performance against different level partners - middle-level and expert unseen partners. The middle-level partner is a commonly used behavior cloning model [6], and the expert partners are strategies of current methods, i.e., SP, PBT, FCP, and MEP, and our proposed \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}}. The experiments showed that \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} outperforms the recent SOTA methods in both evaluation protocols. Additionally, through the analysis of GFGs and P-GFGs, the learning process of \text{COLE}_{\text{SV}} revealed that the framework efficiently overcomes cooperative incompatibility. The contributions in this paper can be summarized as follows.

- We introduce the concept of Graphic-Form Games (GFGs) and Preference Graphic-Form Games (P-GFGs) to intuitively reformulate cooperative tasks, which allows for a more efficient evaluation and identification of cooperative incompatibility during learning.

- We develop the concept of graphic-form gamescapes to help understand the objective and present the COLE framework to iteratively approximate the best responses preferred by most others.

- We prove that the algorithm will converge to the optimal strategy, and the convergence rate will be Q-sublinear when using in-degree preference centrality. Empirical experiments in the game Overcooked verify the proposed algorithm’s effectiveness compared to SOTA methods.
